content: In Michigan, 68% of the total years of potential life lost (YPLL) due to homicide involve Black individuals, compared to 44% nationwide. This disparity is primarily attributed to the higher homicide rate among Black individuals in Michigan compared to the national Black population. Additionally, Black homicide victims in Michigan tend to be slightly younger than White victims. In 1985, the average YPLL per homicide death was 33 years for Black victims, compared to 31 years for White victims. Analyzing descriptive data like this is critical for public health agencies addressing homicide. Furthermore, analytic studies focusing on modifiable risk factors are necessary. At the state level, the high homicide rates have prompted plans to integrate health department and police databases for homicide surveillance. This integration may help identify factors contributing to the elevated homicide rates in Michigan. Since the introduction of the measles vaccine in the United States in 1963, the reported incidence of measles has decreased by 99%, and indigenous transmission has been eliminated in most parts of the country. However, the goal of measles elimination by October 1982 was not achieved. Between 1981 and 1987, annual reported cases ranged from a low of 1,497 in 1983 to a high of 6,282 in 1986. Two major types of outbreaks have been observed recently: those among unvaccinated preschool-aged children, including those younger than the recommended vaccination age of 15 months, and those among vaccinated school-aged children. Large outbreaks among unvaccinated preschool-aged children have occurred in several inner-city areas, with up to 88% of vaccine-eligible children aged 16 months to 4 years being unvaccinated. In these outbreaks, as many as 40% of cases occurred in children under 16 months of age. Surveys in affected areas revealed that only 49%-65% of 2-year-olds had received the measles vaccine. Outbreaks among school-aged children have also occurred in schools with vaccination levels exceeding 98%. These outbreaks have been reported across the country, with attack rates in individual schools ranging from 1% to 5%. Vaccine efficacy in these outbreaks has been high, but primary vaccine failure—where 2%-10% of vaccinated individuals fail to develop immunity—has played a significant role in transmission. Children vaccinated at 12-14 months of age have shown higher attack rates compared to those vaccinated at older ages. In some outbreaks, individuals vaccinated in the distant past, regardless of their age at vaccination, have been at increased risk of disease. However, there is no conclusive evidence that waning vaccine-induced immunity is a major issue. The current measles elimination strategy involves administering a single dose of the measles vaccine at 15 months of age. A documented history of vaccination at or after 12 months of age is considered adequate. The strategy relies on maintaining high immunization levels, careful surveillance, and aggressive outbreak control. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) has periodically reviewed this strategy and progress toward measles elimination. In February 1988, a group of consultants convened by the CDC recommended modifications to the strategy to increase vaccine coverage among preschool-aged children in inner-city areas. The ACIP emphasized the need for research to improve vaccine delivery and considered several changes, including a routine two-dose vaccination schedule and a one-time mass revaccination for school-aged children. To address recurrent measles transmission among preschool-aged children, the ACIP recommends implementing a routine two-dose vaccination schedule in areas with ongoing outbreaks. This includes counties with more than five reported cases among preschool-aged children annually over the past five years. Local officials may choose to implement this schedule selectively in affected parts of a county. In urban areas with recent outbreaks among unvaccinated preschool-aged children, health authorities may also consider adopting this policy. The first dose of the measles vaccine should be administered at 9 months of age or at the first healthcare contact thereafter. Infants vaccinated before their first birthday should receive a second dose at or around 15 months of age. For infants under 1 year of age, a single-antigen measles vaccine is recommended, while the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is recommended for individuals vaccinated on or after their first birthday. Although some evidence suggests that children who do not respond to the first dose administered at a young age may have an altered immune response when revaccinated later, there is no evidence to suggest that these children are not protected from measles. If resources are limited, an acceptable alternative is to lower the age for routine vaccination to 12 months in areas using a single-dose MMR schedule. Other vaccines, such as diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and pertussis vaccine (DTP) and oral polio vaccine (OPV), can be administered simultaneously with the measles vaccine or MMR. For school-based outbreaks, the ACIP recommends revaccination strategies due to the significant role of primary vaccine failure in measles transmission. In outbreaks occurring in junior or senior high schools, colleges, universities, or other secondary institutions, the ACIP advises revaccinating all students and their siblings who received their most recent measles vaccine dose before 1980. This date was chosen to include most students vaccinated between 12 and 14 months of age, a group at increased risk of primary vaccine failure, as the recommended age for routine vaccination was changed from 12 to 15 months in 1976. Additionally, it is easier to identify students by year of vaccination rather than age at vaccination. In some outbreak investigations, students vaccinated before 1978-1980 have been found to be at increased risk for measles, likely due to higher rates of primary vaccine failure associated with older vaccines. These failures may be attributed to suboptimal vaccine storage and handling or the greater instability of vaccines manufactured before the introduction of a new stabilizer in 1979. If revaccinating all students vaccinated before 1980 is not feasible, priority should be given to those vaccinated before 15 months of age. The CDC and Emory University will co-sponsor a course titled Epidemiology in Action, designed for state and local health department professionals. This course, scheduled for May 15-26, 1989, at the CDC, will focus on the practical application of epidemiology to public health issues. It will include lectures, workshops, classroom exercises involving real epidemiologic problems, roundtable discussions, and an on-site community survey.
